name: Mars 1969A and 1969B
short_status: Two identical Soviet Mars orbiters, both destroyed by their Proton rockets six days apart in spring 1969. Neither reached Earth orbit, and the USSR never acknowledged that they existed.
tagline: USSR · Soviet Union · Orbiter · 1969 · Reaching Mars Failure
stats: into flight when the first rocket's third stage shut down and exploded
after liftoff when the second rocket lost an engine

facts.label: First launch
facts.value: 27 March 1969, 10:40:45 UTC (13:40:45 Moscow), Proton-K (8K82K no. 240-01) with a Blok D upper stage (11S824 no. 521L), from Site 81 Pad 23 at Tyuratam (Baikonur)

facts.label: Second launch
facts.value: 2 April 1969, 10:33:00 UTC (13:33 Moscow), Proton-K (8K82K no. 233-01) with Blok D (11S824 no. 522L), from Site 81 Pad 24. RussianSpaceWeb gives the time as 13:30 Moscow, about three minutes earlier than the 10:33:00 UTC figure used here

facts.label: Designations
facts.value: 2M (project M-69) No. 521 and No. 522. Mars 1969A and Mars 1969B are labels applied by NASA's NSSDCA; the launches were never announced by the USSR and the spacecraft were given no Soviet public names

facts.label: Built by
facts.value: NPO Lavochkin, under chief designer Georgy Babakin, with the science payload supplied by the Space Research Institute (IKI) in Moscow

facts.label: Launch mass
facts.value: About 4,850 kg each. Perminov's design history gives a proposed weight of 3,834 kg, but that figure is from the preliminary project and includes a 260 kg lander that was later deleted

facts.label: Structure
facts.value: Built around a single large propellant tank with an internal baffle, with two solar wings totalling 7 square metres, a 2.8 m parabolic high-gain dish, two conical low-gain antennas and three pressurised compartments for electronics, radio and navigation, and cameras. NSSDCA calls the tank spherical; RussianSpaceWeb, describing the 1968 redesign, calls it lenticular with a metal membrane

facts.label: Propulsion and control
facts.value: Turbopump-fed main engine burning nitrogen tetroxide and UDMH, eight attitude thrusters with their own tanks, and three-axis stabilisation using two Sun sensors, two Earth sensors, two Mars sensors, a Canopus sensor, gyros and cold nitrogen gas jets

facts.label: Cameras
facts.value: A film-based system with three cameras, three colour filters and two lenses, storing up to 160 images at 1,024 by 1,024 pixels for a best resolution of 200 to 500 m. NSSDCA describes the lenses as 50 mm (1,500 by 1,500 km field) and 350 mm (100 by 100 km); Perminov and RussianSpaceWeb instead list three telephotometers of 35, 50 and 250 mm focal length

facts.label: Science payload
facts.value: Perminov and RussianSpaceWeb list 13 instruments totalling 99.5 kg for the design as approved, of which 15 kg was carried on the lander that was later deleted. Siddiqi's per-flight instrument list names the RA69 radiometer, an IV1 water vapour detector, a USZ ultraviolet spectrometer, a UTV1 infrared Fourier spectrometer, a KM69 cosmic ray detector, a PL18M solar plasma spectrometer, a RIP-803 low-energy ion spectrometer, a GSZ gamma spectrometer, a UMR2M hydrogen and helium mass spectrometer, D-127 charged particle traps and the three-camera imaging system

facts.label: Planned orbit
facts.value: Capture into roughly 1,700 by 34,000 km at 40 degrees inclination with a 24 hour period, then a burn to lower periapsis to 500 to 700 km for about three months of imaging

facts.label: Planned arrival
facts.value: 11 September 1969 for No. 521 and 15 September 1969 for No. 522, which would have made them the first spacecraft to orbit Mars

facts.label: Lander
facts.value: A 260 kg entry capsule was carried in the design and was to have been released from Mars orbit rather than on approach, but it was deleted before flight because the spacecraft had gained weight and there was no time left for high-altitude balloon drop tests

facts.label: Cause of the first failure
facts.value: The Proton's third stage shut down at T+438.66 s after its turbopump caught fire, traced by RussianSpaceWeb to an imbalance in the pump rotor and by NSSDCA and Siddiqi to a faulty rotor bearing, and then exploded. Siddiqi's NASA chronology gives T+438.46 s. Debris fell in the Altai mountains

facts.label: Cause of the second failure
facts.value: One of the six RD-253 (11D43) first-stage engines failed at T+0.02 s because a drain port in the oxidiser pump cover was missing its hydraulic lock plug, letting oxidiser gas into the cavity and igniting the pump shaft

facts.label: Impact of the second vehicle
facts.value: The rocket flew on five engines for about 25 s, reached roughly 1 km, tipped toward the horizontal, shut down and hit the ground nose first at T+41 s about 3 km from the pad, exploding on impact. The launch complex was essentially undamaged; windows were blown out in the nearby assembly and test building (MIK). NASA's NSSDCA, Siddiqi's NASA chronology and the Russian Wikipedia record of Proton failures all give this sequence independently

facts.label: End of mission
facts.value: Both vehicles were destroyed during launch. No Earth orbit was reached, no telemetry was returned from either spacecraft, and no further M-69 hardware existed to fly in the 1969 window

timeline: IKI hands the science module and data processing system for the second spacecraft to Lavochkin at 11 p.m., less than three months before the launch window opens
The first N1 moon rocket explodes at Baikonur while the M-69 team is on site. The blast blows out the hotel windows and the heating freezes at minus 30 C
NASA launches Mariner 6 toward Mars, four days after the N1 accident
10:40:45 UTC: the first M-69 lifts off from Site 81 Pad 23. The third stage catches fire at T+438.66 s and explodes; debris falls in the Altai mountains
22:22:01 UTC: NASA launches Mariner 7 the same day, and it works
10:33:00 UTC: the second M-69 lifts off from Pad 24. One first-stage engine fails at T+0.02 s and the rocket hits the ground at T+41 s about 3 km away
The date the first spacecraft was to have entered Mars orbit
The date the second spacecraft was to have entered Mars orbit
The M-69 design lineage returns as the M-71 series. The first of the three, Kosmos 419, is stranded in Earth orbit
Mars 2 launches successfully, carrying the instrument set and much of the architecture developed for M-69
Mars 3 launches, the second of the M-71 pair built on the M-69 design lineage
Mariner 9 enters Mars orbit, the first spacecraft to do so, two years and two months after M-69 No. 521 was to have arrived

images.caption: A colour photograph of an M-69 spacecraft standing in a high bay assembly hall with technicians in white coats around it and on a work platform beside it, showing the large spherical propellant tank, the plumbing loop across the body, a solar panel and the parabolic high gain antenna. Wikimedia records the subject as the verification of systems unit for Mars 1969A.
images.credit: Soviet factory photograph, photographer unrecorded; published by NASA/NSSDCA and mirrored on Wikimedia Commons

images.caption: A Soviet design drawing of the АМС «M-69» in two views, with Russian callouts naming the solar panels, the descent vehicle (спускаемый аппарат), the fuel tank, the engine, the parabolic high gain antenna, the instrument compartment, the radiator heater, the omnidirectional antenna, the astro navigation system and the attitude control nozzles. The same drawing is Figure 5 of V. G. Perminov's NASA monograph, captioned there 'The M-69 Spacecraft (Second Version)', where the key is translated into English and item (2) is given as 'lander'.
images.credit: НПО Лавочкина (NPO Lavochkin), via RussianSpaceWeb.com (Anatoly Zak)

images.caption: A small vertical photograph of an M-69 spacecraft part way through assembly, wrapped in protective covers, with the two camera window shrouds and the plumbing loop visible. RussianSpaceWeb captions it 'The Mars M-69 spacecraft during the assembly' and credits NPO Lavochkin.
